Keywords: After, Elinor, Lipper

outputs.L1:
**After Elinor Lipper**

The creature that had once
been a man surrendered his petition,
a stained and grimy scrap,
delivered into the hands of his lord
and master—a petition begging to be
reclassified to the status of a horse.

*You son-of-a-whore,* the master
roared, adding a kick for good measure.
*What is the meaning of this?*

The creature that had once
been a man, having pondered
his petition deeply, replied:

*Were I a horse, I would be granted
one day of rest in ten. As things stand,
I am given none. As a horse,
I might pause now and again
throughout my labor. As a former
man, I may not. As a horse,
I would be asked to perform
work befitting my strength.
As a prisoner, I am forever
hungry, and being hungry, I labor
less and earn less bread, until
I can scarcely stand upright.
A horse is given a stable
and two blankets. I possess
no blankets, and no jacket.
Should a driver strike
a horse too harshly, he is punished,
for a horse is precious. Yet if the brigadiers
beat and kick me, it is no different
than striking a tree. And so you see,
a prisoner is nothing here.
But a horse? A horse is something.*

Within that frozen
and shattered landscape, the plea
carried a ring of truth
audible even to the lord
and master—who had himself
once been a man—and who,
when no other former men could witness it,
affixed that very name to the page,
granting the horse a stable and two blankets.
outputs.L2:
Based on Elinor Lipper

The being who had formerly been a man submitted his written request—a filthy, soiled fragment of paper—placing it before his overlord and ruler. The request sought permission to become a horse instead. "You son-of-a-whore," roared the master, adding a kick for emphasis. "What is the meaning of this?"

Having reflected long and hard upon his appeal, the being who had formerly been a man replied: "Were I a horse, I'd receive a single day of rest for every ten. Right now, I receive none. Were I a horse, I could pause occasionally throughout my labor. Being a former man, I cannot. Were I a horse, my labor would only ever match my physical strength. Being a prisoner, hunger never leaves me, and in my hunger I accomplish less, earn less bread, and can scarcely remain upright. A horse is provided a stable and a pair of blankets. I possess neither blankets nor a coat. Should a driver strike a horse with excessive force, punishment follows, since a horse holds value. Yet when the brigadiers strike and kick me, it's no different from striking a tree. And so you understand—here, a prisoner amounts to nothing. But a horse? A horse holds worth!"

Within that shattered, ice-bound landscape, his argument carried a note of genuine truth—truth perceptible even to his overlord and ruler, who had himself once been a man, and who, at a moment when no other former men were watching, signed that very name upon the paper, thereby awarding the horse both a stable and a pair of blankets.

# A Petition for a Better Life

In one of history's most poignant illustrations of human suffering, a prisoner once submitted a formal petition to his master—not asking for freedom, not pleading for mercy, but requesting to be reclassified as a horse. This single act reveals the profound depths of dehumanization to which he had been reduced, a state so degraded that he no longer aspired to be treated as a man, but merely as a valued animal.

The prisoner's argument was built upon a bitter and undeniable logic. A horse, he observed, enjoyed conditions far superior to his own. The animal was granted rest days when it could recover its strength. It received breaks during the long hours of labor, moments of respite that were never extended to him. And when the working day was done, the horse was given shelter from the elements—a comfort the prisoner could only imagine.

He continued his plea by pointing to the material provisions afforded to the animal. A horse was given a stable to call its own and two blankets to keep it warm through the cold nights. He, by contrast, possessed neither blankets nor even a jacket to shield his body from the harsh weather. The comparison was stark: the beast was clothed and housed, while the man was left exposed and unprotected.

Perhaps most damning of all was his observation about violence and accountability. To beat a horse, he noted, was to invite punishment, for the animal held recognized value and its mistreatment was considered a genuine offense. Yet the abuse he himself endured—the blows, the cruelty, the daily degradation—carried no consequence whatsoever. His suffering was invisible in the eyes of the law and custom that protected even the livestock.

The master who received this petition had once been a man of ordinary life, and something in his own history allowed him to recognize the terrible truth embedded in the prisoner's words. Moved by the undeniable justice of the plea, and perhaps troubled by what it revealed about the world he inhabited, he secretly granted the request. The prisoner was given his stable and his two blankets—a small mercy that, in its very granting, laid bare the monstrous circumstances that had made such a petition necessary in the first place.
outputs.L4:
# The Petition

In the camp where the snow never learned to be gentle,
where men were counted like tools and worn like them too,
there labored a prisoner whose name had been taken,
whose number was all that the ledger still knew.

He had watched, through the long and the merciless winters,
the horses that hauled the same loads that he bore,
and he studied their lives with a strange, quiet envy,
until one gray morning he could bear it no more.

So he sat, in the little he had left of evening,
and he wrote out a petition in careful, plain hand—
not a plea to be freed, for he knew that was hopeless,
but a modest request that his master might grant:

*Let me be reclassified. Let me be counted a horse.*

And below it he laid out his reasons in order,
methodical, sober, impossible to refute:
*The horse, at day's end, is allowed to stop working.
The horse has a stable to shelter its rest.

*The horse has a blanket to keep off the frostbite.
The horse has its ration, measured out to its need.
No man lifts a whip to the horse without reason,
for a horse is a thing that has value indeed.

*I ask for no more than the beast in the traces.
I ask to be worth what an animal's worth.
Grant me the standing, the care, and the mercy
that you would extend to a horse of this earth.*

The master read slowly. And here was the terror:
the master, too, once had been counted a man.
He knew every word of the letter was truthful.
He knew there was nothing at all to withstand.

He could not refuse what the reason had proven.
He could not admit what the granting would mean.
So he folded the paper and, saying nothing,
approved the request where it never was seen.

And there is the horror—not shouted, but whispered:
a system so twisted, so hollowed of grace,
that a man had to beg to be counted as cattle,
and the begging was *reasonable*. That was the case.

For where a horse's life is worth more than a person's,
where dignity's measured in stable and feed,
the deepest indictment is not in the cruelty—
it's that the petition made terrible, undeniable sense.
outputs.L5:
# After Elinor Lipper

Elinor Lipper remains one of the most compelling voices to emerge from the darkest chapters of the twentieth century. Born in 1912, she became known internationally for her firsthand account of life within the Soviet forced-labor system, documented in her memoir *Eleven Years in Soviet Prison Camps*. Her testimony offered readers in the West a rare and unflinching look at the realities of the Gulag.

## Before the Camps

A young woman drawn to communist ideals, Lipper traveled to the Soviet Union with hopes of contributing to what she believed was a just cause. Instead, she found herself arrested during the purges of the 1930s, swept up in the paranoia and repression that defined the era. What followed were more than a decade of imprisonment, hardship, and survival in some of the most remote and brutal corners of the Soviet penal system.

## After the Ordeal

**After** her release and eventual departure from the Soviet Union, Elinor Lipper devoted herself to bearing witness. Her writing did more than recount personal suffering; it served as documentation and warning. In publishing her experiences, she joined a small but crucial group of survivors whose accounts helped shape Western understanding of Soviet realities during a time when many still doubted or dismissed such reports.

Her memoir carried weight precisely because it came from someone who had once believed in the system. That perspective lent her words a particular credibility and emotional force.

## A Lasting Legacy

The story of Elinor Lipper reminds us that history is often preserved through individual courage. **After** everything she endured, she chose to speak rather than remain silent. Her account continues to hold value for historians, students, and anyone seeking to understand how ideology, power, and human resilience intersect.

In remembering figures like Lipper, we honor not only their survival but their determination to ensure that the truth outlived the silence others hoped to impose.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative poem inspired by Elinor Lipper's Gulag memoirs about a prisoner who petitions to be reclassified as a horse.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Petition of Prisoner Number Forty-One**

In the far Kolyma winter, where the breath comes down as glass,
where the numbers wear the faces and the faces have no names,
there was one who kept his ledger of the ways a body dies,
and he added up the columns, and he studied at the sums.

He had seen the horses hauling. He had seen the horses fed.
Seven kilos of the fodder while a man received a crust.
He had seen the horse infirmary, its straw and its warm stall,
where the sick beasts lay recovering that no man might lie down.

For a horse that fell in harness there was inquest and a note,
and a form to sign in triplicate, and someone made to answer;
but a man who fell in harness was a line drawn through a list,
and the frozen ground received him with no question and no grief.

So he wrote it out in pencil on a scrap of cement bag,
in the careful hand of one who had once taught the village school:
*I, the prisoner Forty-One, request to be reclassed,
having noted the advantages, as livestock of the State.*

*I can pull as well as any. I eat less, and I ask
only what you grant the gelding and the mare in the ravine—
the ration and the resting and the roof against the sleet,
and the small consideration that a thing has that has worth.*

The guards, they read it laughing, and they passed it down the line,
and it reached the camp commandant like a joke told twice too far,
and the commandant sat frowning at the pencil and the bag,
for a joke is a small mercy, and he could not spare the mercy.

*Bring him,* said the commandant. And they brought the man inside,
where the stove was breathing softly and the ink pots did not freeze.
*You have written that a horse lives better here than you.
This is slander of the system. Do you stand behind the words?*

And the prisoner said, *Citizen, I have measured it in bread.
I have measured it in mornings that the horses live and men do not.
I am not a clever man. I have only learned to count.
And the arithmetic is finished, and it comes out as I wrote.*

Then the room was very quiet, and the stove went on with breathing,
and the commandant looked out across the wire and past the snow,
where a gray horse in the distance stamped and shook its heavy mane,
and it seemed to him the animal was freer than them both.

*I cannot make you livestock,* said the commandant at last.
*There is no line in the statute. There is no such form to sign.
For a horse is worth a requisition, and a man is only worth
the labor left inside him till the labor is used up.*

And he tore the paper slowly, and he fed it to the stove,
and he watched the words *reclassed* and *livestock* curl to nothing there,
and he sent the prisoner back into the column and the cold,
and he never told a soul, and he was careful not to think.

Now the man went back to hauling, and by spring he too was gone,
and the ground received him quiet with no question and no note,
but the horse survived the winter, for the horse was worth the fodder,
and it pulled the empty sledges over where the graves were not.

And they say—though who is *they* now, in a place the maps forgot—
that his petition traveled outward past the wire, past the guns,
in the mouths of those who lived, in the memory of one
who would write it down in freedom so the reckoning could stand:

that a man once asked in earnest to be counted as a beast,
having proved by simple numbers it would raise him in the world;
and the State, which could do all things, could not grant him even that,
for its cruelty had exceeded what its statutes had foreseen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem "after Elinor Lipper" depicting a labor camp prisoner arguing that a horse's life is better than his own.
counterfactuals.output:
**After Elinor Lipper**

Comrade, do not pity me—
pity the accountant's ledger,
where the horse is written down
in ink that must be answered for.

The horse has worth. When he goes lame
they note it, they investigate.
A man who folds into the snow
is only weather, only fate.

They stable him against the cold.
They ration oats they dare not skip,
for the district demands a horse
returned alive, or someone's slip

becomes a matter for the courts.
But I? I am a self-replacing part.
The train delivers more each spring
than winter empties from the cart.

His harness fits. His load is weighed
so that the beast will last the year.
My back is loaded past the mark—
what breaks in me costs no one dear.

They would not work a horse to death
on purpose; that would be a waste.
A horse is capital, and I
am something cheaper, and displaced.

So when I dream, I dream of hooves,
of being precious, being kept,
of mattering enough that someone
counts me, and, if I died, wept—

not from the tenderness of grief,
but from the fear of what it cost.
To be a thing they must protect.
To be worth more than what I've lost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Turn this historical anecdote from a Soviet prison camp—a man asking to become a horse—into a free verse poem with an ironic, tragic tone.
counterfactuals.output:
**Application for Reassignment**

He stood at the commandant's desk,
cap in his two ruined hands,
and made his request plainly,
the way a man asks for bread
or a day's rest he knows he won't get:

*Comrade, let me be a horse.*

The clerk looked up from his ledger.
Outside, the real horses steamed
in the blue cold of morning,
each breath a small forgiveness
rising toward a sky that did not care.

He had reasoned it all through
in the arithmetic of the starving—
how the horses were led to warm stables,
how they were counted, watered,
how a horse that fell was worth
a report, an inquiry, a name
someone would have to answer for.

A horse was property.
A man was only a number
that the frost could erase for free.

*I would pull the loads,* he said.
*I would ask for nothing
but the oats you give the animals,
the roof, the wall against the wind.
I would be worth more to you
as a horse than I am now.*

And this was the tragedy dressed as a joke,
the joke that no one laughed at:
that in this place he had discovered
the one promotion left to him
was downward, into the harness,
into the honest labor of a beast
that was, at least, allowed to live
because it cost too much to let it die.

They wrote nothing in the ledger.
They sent him back to the trees,
to the two-man saw, the human ration,
the long white indifference of the taiga—

a man who had asked to be a horse
and been refused
even that mercy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a witness account from a forced labor camp, where a dehumanized prisoner requests the status of an animal because animals are treated better.
counterfactuals.output:
**Petition to the Overseer**

I am not asking for my freedom back—
I learned to bury that request years ago,
beneath the frost, beside the men we stack
like split wood when the morning whistles blow.

I ask you only this, and ask it plain:
The horse that draws the ore-cart up the hill,
when its ribs show and it goes lame with strain,
you rest it. You permit the beast to be still.

The camp dogs eat. I've watched them from the line—
the scraps, the marrow, kept from cold at night.
When one falls sick, a hand is laid to sign
its worth. Someone attends. Someone thinks it right.

So make me an animal. Enter my number
in whatever ledger keeps the mules alive.
Grant me the mercy of a good beast's slumber,
the ration measured so a thing survives.

I have forgotten how a name should sound.
I answer to a whistle, to a shove.
I sleep where the dumb creatures sleep, on ground.
Only, they are not worked past what they can bear—

and I am. That is all the difference here.
I do not ask to be a man again.
I ask to matter the way the oxen matter,
to be too costly to be spent like rain.

*—recorded from a survivor's testimony,
name withheld, sector unrecorded*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose-poem about "the creature that had once been a man" who petitions his master to be granted the rights of a horse.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Petition

He came to the threshold on all fours, though he had legs enough to stand, because standing was a thing they'd taught him to forget.

*Master,* he said, and the word came out worn smooth as a river-stone, handled by too many mouths before his own. *I have a petition.*

The master looked up from his ledgers, from his columns of the owned and the owing.

*Speak,* he said, *since you still can.*

And the creature that had once been a man laid down his request like an offering, like the last coin sewn into a hem:

*Grant me the rights of a horse.*

---

*Consider the horse,* he said. *When his labor breaks him, you do not blame him for the breaking. When his legs fail, you do not call it laziness. You feed him not as reward but as maintenance, the way you oil a hinge, and there is a strange mercy in being oiled, in being wanted for your function and not despised for your need.*

*The horse is not asked to be grateful. The horse is not asked to sing while he pulls. No one tells the horse he was born for this and should love the harness. The harness simply is, and the horse simply pulls, and at the end there is a stable, and hay, and the animal dark where no one watches him to see if he is happy.*

*I want the dignity of the beast,* he said. *I have had the dignity of the man, and it was only a longer word for the same yoke, dressed up in the fiction that I chose it.*

---

The master was quiet for a while.

Then he said: *You ask to be lowered.*

*No,* said the creature. *I ask to stop pretending I was ever raised. You made me a man so that my chains would seem like something I deserved. Make me a horse, and at least the chains will just be chains.*

---

This is the terrible thing:

that a soul can be so ground against the millstone of its keeping that it comes to envy the animal—not out of madness, but out of arithmetic. Because the horse is used, but the man is *used and told he is free*, and of the two lies, the second is the one that eats the marrow.

He knelt there, the creature that had once been a man, asking to be demoted into honesty.

And whether the master granted it, the story does not say.

Only that the question hung in the air like breath on a cold morning—

visible for a moment,

then gone,

and the work resumed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
